experiments.name: Symbolic spelling correction before the small formalizer
experiments.kind: preregistered evaluation (inference only, CPU)
experiments.hypothesis: A deterministic dictionary-based spelling correction (Hunspell en_US + ro, keyboard-aware edits, diacritic restoration) applied by the host to the user's message before the formalizer raises tolerant execution equivalence on noisy formalizer-v1 test rows (H1), is non-inferior on clean rows (95% lower bound >= -0.5 points, H2), and as a corrector has precision >= 0.90 and changes <= 1% of clean messages (H3).
experiments.data_version: formalizer-v1 test sha256 b05c76a8…, formalizer-ood-v1 test 09acfb2e…, formalizer-wild-v1 test 077e7164…; corrector tuned on formalizer-v1 dev 86c85e9a…
experiments.conclusions: H1, H2 and H3 hold and the preregistered rule says adopt: a sub-millisecond, logged, deterministic pre-step recovers 3 points on noisy synthetic messages (5-7 on medium/heavy noise, 7.4 on noisy OOD) without touching clean ones. The wild suite shows no net benefit (slightly negative for Romanian), and non-diacritic edits on real text are mostly wrong (jargon, brands, British spelling). Recommendation: adopt only as an optional host pre-step, off by default, with the change log in the reason packet; test a spellfix-v2 (no splits of listed words, technical/brand allowlist, stricter real-traffic edits) as a new preregistered experiment before enabling it by default.
experiments.done: Built lib/spellfix.mjs (spellfix-v1; Hunspell en_US + ro, FrequencyWords 2018 unigrams, keyboard-aware edits, split/merge, diacritic restoration, conservative guards, every change logged), tuned on formalizer-v1 dev only, froze it in the preregistration, measured it on the three sealed suites, then predicted again only the messages it changed (761 formalizer-v1, 227 OOD, 171 wild) with the SmolLM2-135M Q8_0 GGUF on CPU and reused the raw predictions for unchanged rows (rerun control: 300/300 byte-identical). Scored with the same scorers and compared paired.

experiments.done: tools/sop-gbnf.mjs (GBNF of the model surface from the live parser contracts) and tests/sop-gbnf.test.mjs; optional grammar and cache_prompt in lib/formalizer-endpoint.mjs and tools/research/predict-endpoint.mjs; harness tools/research/grammar-constrained-eval.mjs; ceiling tool tools/research/grammar-ceiling.mjs. Stage 1 of 6 cells (135M/360M x wild/OOD/test500), GPU sequential, plus A/A and parser-faithful exploratory conditions; CPU speed on 40 messages x 2.
experiments.results_summary: Primary metric unchanged in all 6 cells (delta 0, 95% [0,0], n=100 each): wild accepted 8%/13%, OOD tolerant exec 27%/42%, test500 80%/84% (135M/360M) with or without grammar. Parse validity on wild 94->99% (135M) and 95->100% (360M), +5 pp [+1,+9]; all 10 repaired outputs were still wrong; wild decision match +4 pp [0,+9] / +5 pp [+1,+10]. CPU speed: median latency ratio 1.19 (135M), 1.00 (360M); GPU < 5%.
experiments.conclusions: Grammar-constrained decoding does not improve accuracy of the small fine-tuned formalizers: with greedy decoding it can only change outputs the grammar rejects, and those (5-8% of wild, <1% elsewhere) become well-formed but stay wrong. It is a cheap validity guarantee (wild parse 99-100%, decision match +4-5 pp), provided the grammar accepts everything the parser accepts; the canonical grammar that forbids leading-blank strings changes 10-14% of OOD outputs without net effect. Recommendation: no accuracy claim; optional always-on guard with a parser-faithful grammar regenerated for the new language; invest in data.

experiments.hypothesis: A mature symbolic NLP pipeline (Stanza EN/RO UD parse) plus deterministic rules (lib/ud-to-sop/) formalizes messages into the current SOP Lang honestly (no invented values; unparsed spans instead of guesses). experiments.results_summary: Frozen v1, current harness, same rows. Tolerant exec: OOD 20.8% (SmolLM2-135M 32.6, 360M 47.6, Haiku no-thinking 49.8); OOD Romanian 21.6% vs 8.0 / 16.9 / 39.0 (vs 135M +13.6 [+7.5,+19.5]); OOD English 20.2 vs 50.9 / 70.4 / 57.8; test sample500 28.8 vs 77.8 / 80.6 (vs 135M -49.0 [-54.1,-43.9]); test Haiku sample 22.0 vs 135M 57.4 / Haiku 36.0. Wild 796: accepted 5.0% (7.3 / 9.5 / 16.1), decision 73.0 (81.5 / 83.9 / 59.3), proposition F1 0.476 (0.569 / 0.557 / 0.541); English rows 0.604 vs 0.631 / 0.610 / 0.628 (differences not decisive). Invented values (dictionary-tolerant anchoring): wild 0.6% vs 40.0 / 26.0 / 18.1%; OOD 0.1% vs 8.4 / 3.2 / 1.5%. Parse validity 100% on every set; unparsed spans in 59% of wild outputs. Distribution gap test->OOD -8.0 [-13.2,-2.6] vs 135M -45.2. Latency p50 38 ms GPU, 217 ms CPU. Exploratory: v1.1 labels layer lifts oracle simple text to 0.46 (test 100) / 0.44 (OOD 100) / wild proposition F1 0.714; gold-free fallback (model output -> rules when a model value is not anchored in the message) OOD 135M 32.6->35.0, 360M 47.6->49.8, Haiku 49.8->50.6, test 135M 77.8->79.8, wild Haiku 0.541->0.595.
experiments.conclusions: H1 refuted, H2 supported, H3 supported, H4 supported, H5 partly (above 135M on Romanian OOD, not decisively above 360M). A mature UD pipeline plus hand-written rules is not a competitive formalizer (it lacks the lexicon-level conventions of the golds, fails on noisy text and has no ambiguity or arithmetic rules), but it is the most honest system measured (verbatim values, 100% parse validity, <1% invention) and it degrades little across distributions. Its role is a host component: repair of unparsed spans and placeholders (verbatim spans, role/preposition classes, dates, numbers), an invention cross-check and fallback for small-model output (+1-2 points gold-free on OOD and test), and a Romanian safety net. The oracle simple-text ceiling (about 0.45 exec) bounds any simplifier in front of it; off-the-shelf rewriters and Haiku do not approach it (eval-rewrite-symbolic-v1).

OOD tolerant exec (287): R 20.6, P-coedit 20.6 (0.0 [-1.4,+1.4]), P-gec 20.9 (+0.3 [-1.4,+2.1]), H 24.0 (+3.5 [-0.7,+7.9]), Hbest 23.0 (+2.4 [-2.1,+7.1]), O 38.7 (+18.1 [+13.1,+23.5]). Test tolerant exec (285): R 35.1, P-gec 36.1 (+1.1 [-1.0,+3.2]), H 35.8 (+0.7 [-4.6,+5.9]), Hbest 29.8 (-5.3 [-10.9,+0.4]), O 55.8 (+20.7 [+15.8,+26.0]); wire F1 R 0.401, H 0.506, O 0.641. Wild (300): proposition F1 R 0.605, P-coedit 0.602, P-gec 0.610, H 0.592 (-1.3 [-6.3,+3.4]), O 0.766 (+16.1 [+11.5,+20.7]); H raises decision match 76.0->85.0 (+9.0 [+4.3,+13.7]), accepted match 8.7->12.7 (+4.0 [0.0,+8.0]) and D1-tolerant all-proposition F1 (+5.6 [+1.4,+9.8]); O decision 98.3, accepted 24.0. Unparsed outputs fall with H/Hbest (wild 49->41%, test 22->12/7%) but correctness does not follow. Name preservation (placeholders restored, none invented): P 95-100%, H 89-92%, Hbest 88-93%. Invented values: R 0.1-0.3%, P 0.4-2.2%, H 0.8-6.3%, Hbest 4.7-6.3%. Answer-like outputs <= 1% except Hbest wild stage 100 (5%). Latency: P 11-17 ms per message on the GPU; H p50 about 2.1 s, Hbest 2.9 s; Haiku cost about 1.0 USD per 1,000 H rewrites and 1.8 USD per 1,000 Hbest calls.
experiments.conclusions: H1 (proofreader helps) not supported: off-the-shelf GEC/CoEdIT models change almost nothing a UD parse depends on (synthetic and wild EN). H2 not supported on the primary metrics; a Haiku rewrite helps the question structure of real messages (decision, accepted match) but not proposition content or execution, and it invents values. H3 refuted: choosing among 4 rewrites by the rules own signals (fewest unparsed) makes outputs easier to parse (unparsed 7-26%) but less correct (test -5.3): pleasing Stanza is not the same as preserving meaning. H4 supported: the oracle simple text gains 16-25 points everywhere. Distilling H or Hbest into a small model is NOT worth training: the teacher itself gains little. The only rewrite target with a large gain is the IR-rendered oracle text, so a simplifier, if any, should be trained on IR->simple-text pairs (the simplifier study plan, questions.md Q-SIMPL-1), and it needs the DS022 labels exactly.

models.name: stronger-judge
models.identity: Claude model fable via the Agent tool, blind, rubric v1

deviations.what: Judge input and procedure fixed on a 30-sentence pilot (the first sentences in sample order) before the full run: (1) the readable rendering gains a mechanical clause-by-clause READING (predicate, subject, objects, obliques with prepositions, negation, attached clauses, noun attachments, question words, entities) above the arc table; (2) the rubric lists valid UD v2 analyses that are not errors (advmod negation, prepositional verbs as obl+case, copula as dependent, xcomp, flat names, lead-ins); (3) a DEEP or FAIL first verdict is re-checked by a second Haiku call (same model, no thinking) that must confirm or drop each claimed arc; the second verdict counts and both are kept. Sentences that the worker labelled Romanian inside English messages (16 of 1216) are not judged (English-only rubric) and are reported apart.
deviations.why: On the pilot, the first prompt flagged valid UD analyses as DEEP (copula heads, look after + obl, advmod negation), which would push rules failures onto the parser.
deviations.effect: The 30 pilot sentences are part of the sample and were re-judged with the final prompt; the pilot verdicts of earlier prompts are discarded. The calibration (a) still measures the final judge against a stronger judge.

deviations.what: Judge rubric v1 replaces rubric v0 after the full v0 run and BEFORE any Layer-1 number was reported: (1) an explicit UD v2 conventions section with examples (copula as dependent, aux under the main verb, passive, xcomp/ccomp/advcl+mark incl. gerund complements, acl:relcl, prepositions and prepositional verbs, question words, STRANDED prepositions as a real error, negation, lead-ins, complex prepositions, how many times); (2) DEEP defined strictly as an analysis that would change the logical form (who did what to whom, polarity, clause structure, question target); (3) every problem gets an issue type: structure, input_typo, ner_type_only, convention_disagreement, minor_label; (4) a fifth verdict INPUT_TYPO: the structure is right and only misspelled input words get non-word lemmas or odd tags (input noise, not a parse error). The second-stage review of DEEP/FAIL is kept with the new rubric. All 1200 sentences are re-judged; the rubric-v0 verdicts are kept in eval/reports/current/symbolic-layers/v0-judge/ for comparison. Layer 3 covers DEEP, FAIL and INPUT_TYPO sentences (spelling is exactly the regularization model's job); the stronger-judge calibration (80 sentences, blind) is run on rubric v1 before any number is reported, and judge precision/recall on DEEP is reported.
deviations.why: Orchestrator spot check of 10 random v0 DEEP verdicts: about half were judge errors (copula/aux expected as root, gerund advcl+mark rejected, input typos counted as parse errors, NER type counted as deep). The stronger-judge calibration launched on v0 was stopped before it judged anything.
deviations.effect: Layer-1 numbers come from rubric v1 only. The v0 distribution (CORRECT 685, MINOR 201, DEEP 297, FAIL 12, unusable 5) is reported only as a judge-validity finding.

deviations.what: Layer-1 final verdicts: the rubric-v1 Haiku judge (1200 sentences: CORRECT 489, MINOR 238, INPUT_TYPO 38, DEEP 418, FAIL 4, unusable 13; the second-stage review downgraded 178 of 604 first DEEP/FAIL) still flags valid UD analyses as DEEP (spot check of 4 copula DEEP verdicts: 3 judge errors). Therefore every sentence Haiku marks DEEP, FAIL, INPUT_TYPO or leaves unusable (433 outside the calibration set) is adjudicated blind by the stronger judge (Claude, model fable, Agent tool, 5 batches, same rubric v1, without Haiku verdicts); the stronger verdict is final for those. Sentences Haiku marks CORRECT or MINOR keep the Haiku verdict; the DEEP miss rate among them is estimated from the 80-sentence blind calibration and reported. Haiku precision and recall on DEEP are reported from the calibration.

experiments.results_summary: Blame (400 msgs, v1.3): correct 32.5%, parser 22.5%, rules 15.3%, rules+convention 13.0%, convention 10.0%, input typo 3.3%, language 1.5%, eval 0 (v1.2: correct 21.3%, rules 24.0%, R+C 20.8%). Layer 1 (1200 sentences, final verdicts): CORRECT 55.6%, MINOR 29.8%, INPUT_TYPO 4.1%, DEEP 10.1% [8.5,11.9], FAIL 0.4%; wild 19.0%, sentences >15 words 32.1%; calibrated estimate 15-17%. Haiku judge vs stronger judge: binary kappa 0.20 [0.00,0.38], DEEP precision 28%, recall 64%. spaCy disagreement predicts DEEP (15.6% vs 4.8%). Layer 2 (273 msgs with correct parses): v1.2 30.0% -> v1.3 46.5%; remaining misses R 113 / C 92 / L 6. Layer 3 (175 DEEP/FAIL/INPUT_TYPO): parse fixed by a rewrite for 59% of DEEP/FAIL and 92% of typos; message saved 18%. Held-out half B: 23.5% -> 32.5%, +9.0 [+5.5,+13.0], 18 gained / 0 lost; wild +0.
experiments.conclusions: Stanza rarely fails outright (0.4%) but about one sentence in ten (one in five on wild, one in three over 15 words) is deeply wrong; still, almost every parser-blamed message also has rules or convention differences. The largest fixable cause was our rules (v1.3 +9 points held out); the second is arbitrary gold conventions (relation/object boundary, per-predicate roles) that need owner decisions (Q-SYM-1/2); the language itself is rarely the gap (Q-SYM-3). Haiku without thinking cannot judge UD parses (kappa 0.20); a stronger judge was needed. A small regularizer should learn spelling, casing, canonical question order and one sentence per list item; stranded prepositions, titles and names need symbolic handling.

experiments.conclusions: SymbolicLM's translate route does not beat direct for Romanian on either measured sample; direct should be the shipped default for Romanian (DEFAULT_ROUTES still sets translate, left as an open item rather than changed silently in a report pass). Language identification, spelling and the uncertainty gate are solid, shippable components on their own. The translator remains useful for its other stated purpose (producing English text for dataset_proofing and any future English-side proofreading model), and for mixed Romanian/English messages, where the exploratory result favors translate but is not yet decided. Two named losses from the paused run (Oare, impersonal se) were already fixed in the frozen code before this report; the Context:/Intrebare: two-clause pattern (2.6% of the sealed OOD suite) is a genuine lib/ud-to-sop rules gap, left open rather than patched around in the translator.

earlier_heuristic_run.conclusions: On this small (n=40/bucket), heuristic-only cross-check: the already-shipped, free, in-process symbolic backend (LanguagesUtil spellfix + TranslatorService dictionary translation) has the best or tied-best meaning preservation on every bucket (noisy_en 100%, mixed 82.5%, ro 72.5%) and is comfortably inside the ~2s UI budget (57-509ms), at the cost of a lower fully-English rate on Romanian (65%, i.e. some untranslated dictionary gaps remain visible to the user). experiments.hypothesis: Principled KnowledgeLinker repairs (role relabeling, converse frames, frame tier, boundary shift, article stripping) and a dev/sealed split improve open-vocabulary linking on world-v1 + core-en without raising the wrong-link rate; circuit rules reach the chat turn.

results.hypotheses: H1 yes on the direction (sealed scored over exact +6.2 points; dev over the M3 half +1.3 points on all rows, +6.2 on English rows) but far from the section 6.2 targets; H2 partly (unjustified 34.0% sealed against 44.8% exact; not under 5%); H3 not met (wrong-link 12.1% against 1% target; it is dominated by generic verbs bound where the memory has no facts); H4 confirmed in direction on the sealed half.

deviations: The memory changed under the evaluation: worldkb-agent remapped world-v1 onto core-en predicates during the task, and the english-core-agent made the core English-only. Labels judged against the old vocabulary are read through PREDICATE_RENAMES (one-to-one renames) in tools/eval/linking-open.mjs. Romanian rows (about one in eight) score 0 by design after the owner decision (translate at the edges); the report gives the English rows apart (by_language).

The M3 linker could not be run on the new memory, so H1 to H3 are compared with the M3 numbers of the same half measured before the work (dev 36.1% relation, 14.8% wrong-link, 35.3% unjustified) and with the exact arm on the new memory.
No new LLM labels were needed (no judge calls).
